newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong bows to reality and lowers GDP forecast.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong bows to reality and lowers GDP forecast.

text.p: The Hong Kong government bowed to reality on Friday and revised down its economic growth forecast for 1996.
Some economists said they economy might even have a hard time reaching the reduced figure, although others believed the government was unreasonably pessimistic in its forecast.
The government revised its real gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast for the year to 4.7 percent from 5.0 percent and cut its inflation forecast to 6.8 from 7.5 percent.
It also estimated second quarter GDP growth at just over four percent, up from 3.1 percent in the first three months of 1996, and predicted it would pick up in the second half.

"The figures show the financial secretary had to be persuaded to drop the forecast rate and they've settled on this in-between figure, between 5.0 and 4.5," chief economist Ian Perkin at the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce said.
"But I think 4.7 is going to be difficult to achieve, too, unless you get five to six percent in the final half," he said.
Financial Secretary Donald Tsang made light of the revision as he toured New Zealand on Friday. "4.7 is on the trend line of 5.0," he said.
Tsang blamed the shift on weaker than expected trade in the first six months, which he described as "not brilliant at all".
But he said not only Hong Kong suffered on that front. "In the entire East Asia economies, every finance minister has been reducing their forecasts because of that."
He speculated the lacklustre external trade position may have been a result of currency movements. "But to me it is still looking pretty good," he said.

Perkin was sceptical. "I'm not at all convinced that consumption can get much better...and I can't see growth in trade picking up much either," said Perkin, who three months ago predicted GDP growth of four percent as more reasonable.
"The latest indications from the United States are there may need to be an interest rate rise before year-end and that would have a negative effect on the Hong Kong economy," he said.
But Andrew Freris, chief regional economist at Salomon Brothers, remained upbeat.
"This was not unexpected but it's unduly pessimistic and extremely narrowly focused. The revision is extremely selective and concentrates on trade," Freris said.
"We remain bullish on the Hong Kong economy for 1996 and we are not adjusting our forecast of 5.2 percent," he said.
Freris said he saw a continuing recovery of consumption and a mild improvement of the external balance.

Nicholas Kwan, senior economist at Merrill Lynch, agreed with the government's forecast. "We have been looking at 4.7 for some three months already now, so I guess it's a move towards reality," Kwan said.

He said his department was still calculating inflation for the year at 7.2 percent, slightly higher than the government forecast. "But that still shows there is a generally down trend and that there's not so much pressure on prices."
On August 1 Hang Seng Bank also cut its forecast for GDP growth to 4.5 from 4.8 percent. Other forecasters have set figures as low as 3.9 percent.
In its last quarterly forecast on May 31 the government held firm to its 5.0 percent forecast dating from March, despite scepticism from some economists that the rate was achievable.
